planting.note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, mineral cactus mix, or plant rooted offsets in spring into sharply drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; ladyfinger cactus is native to the brushlands of South Texas and northern Mexico and forms sprawling mats of slender, finger-like stems.

directions: Plant in sharply drained, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; ladyfinger cactus is a low, sprawling native of the South Texas brushlands and adjacent Mexico, its slender, finger-thick stems rooting where they touch the ground to form a loose, spreading mat rather than an upright clump. In spring it produces a spectacular flush of large, satiny, magenta-pink flowers with a darker throat, often nearly covering the plant for several days at a time, among the showiest blooms of any native hedgehog cactus. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than more northern Echinocereus species and performs best in the milder winters of zones 8 to 10, where it makes an excellent groundcover for a rock garden, gravel bed, or the sunny, well-drained edge of a xeriscape planting. Good drainage is essential, since standing winter moisture quickly rots the shallow-rooted stems.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, mineral cactus mix, or plant rooted offsets in spring into sharply drained, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun; Texas pitaya forms large sprawling mounds and is grown both as an ornamental and for its sweet, strawberry-flavored fruit.

directions: Plant in sharply drained, rocky or gravelly, lean soil in full sun; Texas pitaya is a robust, clump-forming hedgehog cactus native to the Chihuahuan Desert and South Texas brushlands, forming large sprawling mounds of thick, blue-green stems that can eventually spread several feet across. Large magenta-purple flowers open in mid-spring, followed by egg-sized, spiny red fruit that ripens in early summer and, once the spines are removed, has a sweet flavor reminiscent of strawberries — long harvested by regional residents as a wild treat, giving rise to the Spanish common name pitaya. It is more cold-hardy than many South Texas cacti and tolerates the milder winters of zones 7 through 10 as long as drainage is excellent, making it a good dual-purpose ornamental and fruiting choice for a xeriscape or rock garden planting.
